extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate computer science and mathematics students (Don Knuth's class) preparing term papers, articles, and mathematical exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and presenting mathematical and CS expository work (term papers, articles, proofs), covering quotation selection, exposition techniques, typographic/notation conventions, proof-construction methods, and interaction with editors/proofreaders. Aimed at improving clarity, pedagogy, and publication readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective use of quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote only when quoted words convey your meaning better than you can, are beautiful/witty, will touch a chord of association in readers, or you wish to preface/conclude with an apt aphorism. Avoid quoting merely to show you are learned (pretentious quotation is ill-advised).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons to quote: clarity, beauty, association, epigraph. Anti-pattern: quoting to impress—discerning readers detect and resent it. Examples: Bartlett and OED as sources; Don's practice of finding apt aphorisms to preface chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic methods for locating quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation dictionaries (Bartlett), the OED (which prints memorable quotations), concordances (Shakespeare/Chaucer), and online searchable texts to find appropriate quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When serendipity fails, search indexes and concordances; use computer searches (when texts are available online) to find occurrences of keywords. Example: searching online text for 'comma' to find quotation about punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable liberties with quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acceptable to take quotations out of context, to quote yourself, to repurpose a quote from an unrelated topic, or to solicit a remark from an expert for epigraphic use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: using Leontief on (economic) output in a chapter on (computer) output; quoting explorers or obscure sources when relevant. Caution: ensure the repurposing doesn't mislead readers about the original meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexing and bibliographic habits
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide and check good indexes for long works; consult indexes systematically (if not found in the index, check the work carefully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Sears & Roebuck advice and Lord Campbell's wish for compulsory indexing. Practical tip: an index improves usability; authors should ensure index accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph and page-level typography aesthetics
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to paragraph indentation and the visual balance of page lines; sometimes add or subtract words so the last line of a paragraph is at least as long as the indentation of the next paragraph to avoid odd page appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a subtle typographic aesthetic—authors or editors may need to reword to achieve pleasing line-end lengths. Anti-pattern: leaving pages with jarring short final lines that disrupt reading flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotations as intentional rhetorical devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Select quotations to preface or conclude chapters or sections to set tone, introduce themes, or provide ironic counterpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don took pleasure finding 'really good aphorism' to preface pieces. When chosen well, quotations can frame reader expectations and enhance stylistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to rework prose for a general audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing for a broad readership, remove or reduce jargon and technicalities and be open to editorial changes aimed at accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Don's Scientific American article was heavily edited to suit general readers; although some edits felt gratuitous, cooperation ultimately made the article more accessible. Practical tip: negotiate on technical points but accept substantive readability improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate and check proofs carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must review page proofs meticulously because typesetters and copy editors often introduce errors, especially in technical material (mathematical symbols, brackets, numerals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: printers misrendering '0' and '1' as other symbols, bracket vs parentheses swaps, substitution of words that change meaning. Practical step: insist on proofs when heavy technical typesetting is involved and correct errors before final printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about notation conventions (avoid ambiguous symbols)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose notation deliberately and state conventions (e.g., 'lg' for log base 2 vs 'log' ambiguity); be consistent about bracket types and numeric formatting in formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: IEEE changed 'lg' to 'log' causing base confusion; authors object to comma insertion in formula numbers (1,000,000) and prefer 1000000 or 10^6; IEEE uses space grouping (1 234 567) in numeric tables. Guidance: pick a convention appropriate to the venue and audience and defend it if crucial to meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sensitive to grammatical choices in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Some words (e.g., 'data') are used both singularly and plurally; choose usage suitable to context and audience and be prepared to accommodate editors' preferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: editors changed 'data has' to 'data have'—Don accepted 'data must' as compromise. Practical tip: prioritize clarity and audience expectations over pedantry, but be prepared to justify unusual usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide when to display equations for clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether to include displayed equations: some venues (e.g., Scientific American) avoid displayed equations for a general audience; readers may object if equations are omitted when helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance: avoid intimidating non-technical readers, but don't remove necessary formalism that conveys essential meaning. If equations are typographically challenging, insist on proof review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an expository format that suits the material
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue, Q&A, or question-and-answer formats can be effective expository devices for presenting ideas (examples: Lamport's Q&A format, Don's 'Surreal Numbers' dialog).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such formats can make difficult ideas more approachable and engaging; they are legitimate alternatives to traditional formal exposition when used purposefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and puzzles to motivate complex results
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a concrete example or puzzle that builds the right mental structures in the reader's mind before presenting the algorithm or formal proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the algorithm presented is not optimal or contains many cases, the example primes the reader to understand why the problem is nontrivial and how the solution direction arises. This is a pedagogical technique for exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance formal and informal discussion; choose typographic conventions to aid comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Blend formal definitions and informal explanations with well-chosen examples; adopt typographic conventions (e.g., typewriter font for logic) that clarify distinctions between meta-language and object language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Nilsson & Genesereth's chapter praised for mixing formal/informal discussion and clear typographic cues. Good exposition uses formatting to reduce reader cognitive load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphor and domain-specific terminology to explain complex constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof or construction is complicated, provide an extended metaphor and convenient terminology (e.g., the 'jellyfish' metaphor: stems, polyps, tentacles, heads, nematocysts) to help readers form intuitive models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Naming and metaphors aid comprehension and recall; however, choose names carefully because they may become permanent. Community consensus (polls) sometimes drives preferred terminology (e.g., 'NP-complete').

rubrics_metrics.name: Carefully construct existence/sequence proofs with well-definedness and uniqueness checks
rubrics_metrics.description: When constructing sequences or functions (e.g., via diagonalization) ensure selections are well-defined (no ambiguity from repeated indices), that enumerations cover required sets, and verify that the constructed object has the asserted property (e.g., In is well-defined because ni ≠ nj).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the proof: use diagonalization to choose ordered pairs with strictly increasing first components; define functions by cases (if n = n_k then value t_k, otherwise default) and check consistency; use contrapositive arguments to prove properties like 'if infinitely many In(S) ≠ R then S is countable.' Anti-pattern: leaving definitions ambiguous or failing to check that constructed choices satisfy uniqueness/inclusion conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a genre in mind for term papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pick a genre for your term paper (expository, research note, humorous spoof, etc.) and do a good job within that genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Don recommended having a genre in mind and referenced Woody Allen spoof as a stylistic example. Practical tip: genre guides structure, tone, expected conventions, and audience expectations.
